specPoints.text: describe how current varies with voltage in wires, resistors, metal filament lamps and diodes, and how to investigate this experimentally
describe the qualitative effect of changing resistance on the current in a circuit

primer.text: How a component responds to voltage is easiest to see as a graph. A straight line through the origin means steady, predictable behaviour; a curve means the component is changing underneath you. This note reads the IV graphs of wires, filament lamps and diodes, then shows the bench setup that measures them and the resistance dial that controls them.

lessons.title: IV graphs
sourceHeadings: IV graph for a wire or a resistor
lessons.opening: Plot the current through a component against the voltage across it and the shape of the line tells you everything. Straight through the origin: the resistance never budges. Curved away: something inside is changing. This lesson learns to read both shapes and names the components that produce them.
keyPoints: An IV graph plots the current through a component against the voltage across it.
A straight line through the origin means the relationship is linear and the resistance stays constant.
A curved graph means the resistance changes as the current varies.
Wires and fixed resistors at steady temperature give linear, directly proportional graphs.
Filament lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors all produce non-linear graphs.

low.restatement: Straight-line graph: same resistance however hard you push. Curved graph: the resistance is drifting.
low.analogy: A spring scale versus a stiffening hose: one reads the same every pull, the other fights back harder the more you open it.
low.examPointer: The word 'origin' matters — a straight line that misses the origin is not the proportional case.

medium.restatement: Direct proportionality means doubling one quantity doubles the other, which is exactly what a straight line through the origin encodes.
medium.analogy: A taxi meter with a fixed rate: twice the distance, twice the fare, forever on the same straight line.
medium.examPointer: At constant temperature is the exam qualifier for a fixed resistor's line — quote it when describing the linear case.

check.stem: An IV graph that is a straight line through the origin shows:

options.text: a resistance that grows with voltage
options.explanation: A growing resistance would bend the line, not keep it straight.
The straight proportional line is the signature of unchanging resistance.
Reverse bias shows a flat zero region, not a rising straight line.
A rising line records current growing with voltage.

check.stem: Which component gives a linear IV graph at constant temperature?

options.explanation: The lamp's graph bends as its filament heats.
The diode's graph is strongly non-linear.
At steady temperature a fixed resistor's straight line passes through the origin.
An LDR's resistance moves with the light level.

check.stem: On a non-linear IV graph, the resistance:

options.explanation: Constancy is the straight-line signature, not the curved one.
The curvature exists precisely because the resistance varies.
A zero resistance would be a vertical line, not a curve.

options.text: cannot be found at any point
options.explanation: Reading voltage and current at a point still gives the resistance there.

check.stem: For a wire at steady temperature, doubling the voltage across it:

options.explanation: Direct proportionality: twice the push, twice the flow.
That falloff belongs to heating components like filament lamps.
Voltage is what drives the current through the wire.
That acceleration belongs to a forward-biased diode, not a wire.

check.stem: Which statement about the resistance of a wire at constant temperature is true?

options.explanation: Rising resistance with current is the filament's behaviour, not a cool wire's.

options.text: it falls as the voltage rises
options.explanation: Nothing in a steady-temperature wire lowers its resistance.

options.text: it depends on the voltmeter used
options.explanation: The resistance belongs to the wire, not the meter.

options.text: it stays constant as the voltage varies
options.explanation: A steady-temperature wire keeps one resistance across the voltage range.

check.stem: What shape does the IV graph of a fixed resistor take, and what does the shape tell you?
check.modelAnswer: A straight line through the origin — the current is directly proportional to the voltage, so the resistance stays constant.

check.stem: Name two components with non-linear IV graphs.
check.modelAnswer: Filament lamps and diodes — thermistors and LDRs are non-linear too.

check.stem: Explain what an IV graph running straight through the origin tells you about how the current behaves.
check.modelAnswer: Current and voltage grow in step, so doubling one doubles the other — the current is directly proportional to the voltage and the resistance never changes.

check.stem: A fixed resistor's IV graph passes through (2 V, 0.4 A) as a straight line through the origin. Predict the current at 5 V, then the resistance.
check.modelAnswer: The line's steepness sets the ratio: current per volt = 0.4 ÷ 2 = 0.2 A per volt, so 5 V gives 5 × 0.2 = 1 A. The resistance is 2 ÷ 0.4 = 5 Ω.

lessons.title: IV graph for a filament bulb
sourceHeadings: IV graph for a filament bulb
lessons.opening: Two stars of the non-linear world. The filament lamp heats itself as it works, and its own heat throttles it back. The diode is a one-way valve — generous forwards, immovable backwards. This lesson reads both graphs and the physics that shapes them.
keyPoints: A filament lamp's graph bends over: the current grows more slowly than the voltage.
The rising current heats the filament, and hotter lattice atoms obstruct the electrons more.
So the lamp's resistance increases as the current grows.
A diode passes current in one direction only — the forward-bias direction.
In reverse bias a diode's resistance is extremely high and effectively no current flows.
On the diode's graph, forward bias shows a sharp rise on one side and reverse bias shows a flat zero region.

low.restatement: Lamp: the graph flattens as it warms, because heat adds resistance. Diode: current one way, blocked the other.
low.analogy: The lamp is a runner tiring as they go; the diode is a turnstile that spins one way and locks the other.
low.examPointer: Name the mechanism — hot filament, vibrating atoms — not just the curve, when asked to explain the lamp's graph.

medium.restatement: The lamp's slowdown is negative feedback: more current heats the filament, and the heat raises the resistance that restrains the current.
medium.analogy: A self-regulating door that gets heavier the harder you push it — progress continues, but always a little less easily.
medium.examPointer: For non-linear graphs, resistance at a point is voltage divided by current at that point — the straight-line gradient shortcut does not apply.

check.stem: As the voltage across a filament lamp increases, the current:

options.text: increases at a proportionally slower rate
options.explanation: The growing resistance bends the graph, so the current gains less and less.

options.text: increases at a proportionally faster rate
options.explanation: The lamp's rising resistance restrains the current instead.
Proportionality is the cool fixed resistor's behaviour.
The current still grows; only its rate slows.

check.stem: The filament's resistance grows with current because:

options.text: the filament's temperature rises and its atoms vibrate more
options.explanation: Hotter lattice atoms obstruct the drifting electrons, raising the resistance.
No mass leaves the wire in normal operation.
The resistance rises rather than being destroyed.
Charge carriers are never manufactured by the current.

check.stem: In reverse bias, a diode:

options.explanation: Large current belongs to forward bias.
Blocking is normal diode behaviour, not damage.
The reverse side of a diode graph is a flat zero region.

options.text: has a very high resistance and passes essentially no current
options.explanation: The reverse direction is the diode's blocked direction.

check.stem: A diode conducts:

options.explanation: The whole point of a diode is its asymmetry.
Forward bias conducts freely.
Forward bias passes current; reverse bias blocks it.
Diode behaviour is about direction, not alternation.

check.stem: Compared with a fixed resistor's graph, a filament lamp's graph:

options.explanation: The lamp's heating makes its graph bend.

options.text: bends as the resistance climbs with temperature
options.explanation: The curve records the growing resistance of the hot filament.
Current still grows with voltage; the slope stays positive.

options.text: never passes through the origin region at all
options.explanation: Both graphs start near zero and rise from there.

check.stem: Describe the shape of a filament lamp's IV graph and state what happens to its resistance.
check.modelAnswer: The graph curves so the current rises more slowly than the voltage; the lamp's resistance increases as the filament heats.

check.stem: What is forward bias for a diode?
check.modelAnswer: The direction in which the diode lets current flow — when the current lines up with the arrowhead of the symbol.

check.stem: Explain why a diode passes no current in reverse bias.
check.modelAnswer: In reverse bias the diode's resistance becomes extremely high, and a very large resistance chokes the current to effectively zero.

check.stem: A diode is placed in a circuit backwards. State what the ammeter reads and what the IV graph shows on that side.
check.modelAnswer: The ammeter reads zero, and the graph lies flat along the axis on the reverse side, showing the very high reverse resistance.

lessons.title: Investigating current and voltage
sourceHeadings: Investigating the relationship between current and voltage
lessons.opening: Graphs do not draw themselves. Bench practice: adjust the current with a variable resistor, read the voltage off a voltmeter, and record the pairs. Step the current up, plot what you collected, and the component's IV curve appears. This lesson walks the setup and the resistance dial behind it.
keyPoints: The investigation needs an ammeter, a voltmeter, a variable resistor, a power source and wires.
The variable resistor adjusts the current, which is the independent variable.
The voltmeter reads the voltage across the component — the dependent variable.
Recording current and voltage pairs while stepping the current up yields the component's IV graph.
A higher resistance in a circuit means a smaller current; a lower resistance means a larger one.
Fixed resistors keep one resistance; variable resistors change theirs by altering the wire length in circuit.

low.restatement: Set the current with the variable resistor, read the voltage, step, repeat — the pairs plot the graph.
low.analogy: Tuning a radio dial (variable resistor), noting the volume (voltage) at each setting, then plotting the response.
low.examPointer: Independent variable = what you set (current); dependent variable = what you measure (voltage). Get the labels right for the marks.

medium.restatement: The variable resistor is the experiment's steering wheel: lengthening its wire raises resistance and eases the current down for the next reading.
medium.analogy: A dimmer slider on a lamp — slide it and the brightness steps smoothly through the range you want to record.
medium.examPointer: Quote the resistance-current see-saw (higher resistance, smaller current) for the qualitative-effect part of the question.

check.stem: In the IV investigation, the independent variable is:

options.explanation: Voltage is the quantity read off — the dependent variable.

options.text: the current, adjusted with the variable resistor
options.explanation: The experimenter sets the current, making it independent.
The ammeter's resistance is assumed negligible and fixed.
Wire length is inside the variable resistor, not the measured variable.

check.stem: The instrument that varies the current in the investigation is the:

options.explanation: The ammeter measures the current; it does not set it.
The voltmeter measures the voltage across the component.
Adjusting the variable resistor steps the current through the circuit.
The source provides the push; the resistor does the adjusting.

check.stem: Increasing a circuit's resistance while the supply stays fixed makes the current:

options.explanation: More opposition at the same push means less flow.
That would need less resistance, not more.
Resistance is the dial that controls the current.
Direction of flow has nothing to do with the resistance size.

check.stem: A variable resistor changes its resistance by:

options.explanation: Self-heating is the filament's story, not the variable resistor's control method.

options.text: altering the length of wire in the circuit
options.explanation: Sliding the contact changes how much wire the current must traverse.
Cells change the supply voltage, not the resistor.
Direction does not set a resistor's value.

check.stem: A longer variable-resistor wire gives:

options.explanation: More wire means more opposition, not less.
The whole point of the slider is a changing resistance.
Wire never offers zero resistance in reality.
A longer wire carries more opposition for the charge to pass.

check.stem: List the equipment needed to investigate how current varies with voltage.
check.modelAnswer: An ammeter, a voltmeter, a variable resistor, a power source and connecting wires.

check.stem: State which quantity is the independent variable in the IV investigation and which instrument changes it.
check.modelAnswer: The current is independent, and the variable resistor is used to change it.

check.stem: Explain why the voltmeter's readings form the dependent variable of the investigation.
check.modelAnswer: The experimenter sets the current with the variable resistor and then reads off the voltage that results, so the voltage depends on the chosen current.

check.stem: An investigator steps the current up five times, recording the voltage each time. What can be plotted from the pairs, and which shape signals a constant resistance?
check.modelAnswer: The recorded pairs plot an IV graph; a straight line through the origin signals a constant resistance.

glossary.definition: A plot of the current through a component against the voltage across it.
Describing a straight-line relationship through the origin, where quantities grow in step.
Describing a curved relationship, where the resistance varies as the current changes.
The pattern where doubling one quantity doubles the other, drawn as a straight line through the origin.
A light source whose wire heats as it works, so its resistance rises with current.
A component that passes current in one direction only.
The diode direction that conducts, aligned with the symbol's arrowhead.
The diode direction that blocks, where the resistance is extremely high and no current flows.
